6.text: of the secluded beauty. They were kept, not in the iron box, but in the

7.text: large sleeping-room of their father’s house. When talked to by strange men,

8.text: they pretended to be shy, and not inclined to conversation. Even the color

9.text: of their face grew more delicate and white, as becomes a secluded beauty.

10.text: All their time and attention were given to needle-work on soft, spotted skins.

11.text: Of those skins they prepared man’s clothes of the best quality. Of course

12.text: these clothes were sold to American whalers in exchange for sugar, flour, and

13.text: cheap brandy, which does not correspond to the description given in tales.

14.text: The other type of Chukchee bride, as described in tales, corresponds

15.text: more closely to the conditions of Chukchee life. She is strong and proud.

16.text: Not either of her parents, but she herself, shows resistance to the suitor.

17.text: She has to be sought for and conquered by strength and courage.

18.text: In one tale the bride is described as living in a single house with her

19.text: old parents. She refuses all suitors. Being very swift of foot, she invites

20.text: them to a foot-race, in which they are defeated. Then they are sent home.

21.text: At last a young man comes to her house. He drives his spear into the

22.text: ground in front of the door, and enters. The girl is not there. Her father

23.text: inquires, “Why have you come?” — “I am a suitor.” — “We have a daughter;
